opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's changed quite a lot, honestly. When I started my PhD, around the time we were working on things like neural task programming and regression planning networks, the motivation was pretty clear. Robots needed to do long-horizon tasks, and pure end-to-end learning just wasn't getting there. Symbolic structure gave you compositionality, generalization to new goals, and some interpretability. So the bet was that we should learn the parts that are hard to hand-engineer, like perception and low-level skills, and keep some symbolic scaffolding for reasoning and planning.

What I didn't fully anticipate was how much large language models would shift the picture. In a way, language turned out to be the symbolic layer we were looking for, except it's much richer and you don't have to hand-design the predicates and operators. Before, a lot of the pain in neural-symbolic work was defining the symbols. What counts as "on," what counts as "grasped," how you ground those in pixels, and what happens when the world doesn't fit your ontology. Language models basically give you a huge, flexible, pre-trained abstraction space for free.

So my view moved from "we need carefully engineered symbolic structure plus learning" to "we need structure, but it can be soft, learned, and expressed in language or code." I still believe the core intuition: long-horizon behavior needs some kind of abstraction and hierarchy. You don't want to reason about every joint torque when you're deciding to clean up a kitchen. But where that abstraction comes from has changed.

At the same time, I've become a bit more cautious about overclaiming on the language side. Language is great for high-level reasoning, but a lot of what makes manipulation hard isn't verbalizable. How much force to apply, how a deformable object behaves, the subtle contact dynamics. That knowledge lives in data and in the low-level policy, not in a symbolic plan. So the bottleneck has shifted down the stack. Ten years ago the question was how do we plan over long horizons. Now, planning at the language level is somewhat solved, and the hard part is getting robust, general low-level skills, which is why so much of my attention has moved toward data, things like scalable data collection and learning from human demonstrations.

If I had to summarize: I still think structure matters, but I'm much less attached to it being hand-designed and explicitly symbolic. The interesting question now is what the right interface is between the reasoning layer and the physical layer, and how they can learn from each other rather than one just issuing commands to the other.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses how LLMs changed his view, but does not identify the RT series or say this work showed the direction remained too far from realization.

r002.rationale: The candidate says language is useful for high-level reasoning and discusses the reasoning-to-physical interface; it does not judge deliberately grounding language in action to be unpromising.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, my view has shifted quite a bit, and I think the honest answer is that I was more optimistic about the explicit neural-symbolic story early on than I am now, but I've also become more appreciative of what it was trying to get at.

When I started working in this space, the appeal of the symbolic side was very concrete. Robotics has these long-horizon tasks, and purely end-to-end neural policies just fell apart once you went beyond a few steps. So the natural thing was to say, let's have a structured representation in the middle. A planning language, a task graph, something like PDDL-style predicates, and let the neural components handle perception and low-level control while the symbolic layer handles compositionality and reasoning. That was a really clean division of labor, and I genuinely believed it was the way to get generalization.

What changed for me was partly watching what large language models did. Suddenly you had a system that could do a lot of the compositional, high-level reasoning that we had been trying to hand-engineer into symbolic structures, except it did it in natural language, with all the messiness and flexibility that comes with that. And the interesting thing was that it didn't need us to define the predicates ahead of time. That was always the Achilles' heel of the neural-symbolic approach in robotics. Someone had to decide what the symbols were, and the moment the real world didn't fit the vocabulary you picked, the whole thing got brittle.

So I think the first shift was realizing that language is kind of the symbolic layer, just not in the rigid form we expected. It's a learned, fuzzy, hugely expressive symbol system, and it comes with priors about the world baked in from pretraining.

But I'd push back on the idea that this means the symbolic intuition was wrong. If anything I think the core insight survived. You still want abstraction. You still want something that lets you decompose a task, reason about preconditions and effects, verify that a plan makes sense before you execute it. What's changed is where that structure comes from. Instead of a human writing down a domain, we're increasingly seeing structure emerge from models, or we're using language models to generate the structure on the fly, things like writing code as a plan, or producing intermediate representations that are grounded by a learned module.

The second thing I've become more cautious about is grounding. The language model can produce a beautiful plan, but the gap between "pick up the mug" as a token and actually picking up the mug with a real gripper in a cluttered kitchen is where most of the hard work still lives. For a while I think the community, myself included, got a bit seduced by how good the high-level reasoning looked and underestimated how much the symbolic layer was papering over physical grounding problems. The failures aren't usually in the reasoning anymore. They're in the interface between the abstract description and the continuous world.

So where I've landed is something like this. I think of language and structure less as a fixed architecture choice and more as a tool for data, supervision, and interpretability. Language is incredibly useful for specifying tasks, for giving feedback, for letting humans inspect what the robot thinks it's doing. The symbolic ideas are useful for giving us handles to verify and compose behaviors. But I no longer believe the robot's internal representation needs to be symbolic in a classical sense for any of that to work. The representation can be learned, and the structure can be something we impose at the boundaries, when we train it and when we talk to it, rather than something hardwired in the middle.

And I'll admit there's some humility in that. Some of the early work, including my own, was trying to engineer the right abstraction. Now I spend more time thinking about how to get enough of the right data and the right feedback so the abstraction can be learned, and how to keep enough structure around to trust the result. That feels like a more durable framing to me, even if it's less elegant than the original neural-symbolic picture.

r001.rationale: The response discusses changing views and grounding challenges, but does not identify the RT series or say it showed the direction remains far from realization.

r002.rationale: It describes grounding language in physical action as difficult, but does not judge deliberate language-to-action grounding to be an unpromising path for robotics.

astra-6.text:
My view has shifted from thinking about neural-symbolic methods as a particular architecture to thinking more about what structure actually helps a robot learn and act. Language is useful for expressing goals and breaking a task into steps, but naming those steps doesn’t solve the grounding problem. The robot still has to connect them to what it sees and what it can physically do.

So I’m less attached to having a clean boundary between a neural component and a symbolic component. I’m more interested in whether the system can use that structure when it’s helpful, learn from experience, and revise its plan when something doesn’t work. The exciting direction, to me, is connecting high-level reasoning to that feedback loop.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention the RT series or say that this work showed the direction was still too far from realization.

r002.rationale: The response describes connecting high-level reasoning to feedback as an exciting direction, rather than judging deliberate language grounding in action as unpromising.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become less attached to a particular architecture and more focused on what the robot actually needs. The appeal of the neural-symbolic approach is that language gives you a way to describe a task at a high level, and symbolic structure can help you break it into steps. But saying “pick up the cup” doesn’t solve the problem of actually picking up the cup. You still need perception, control, and the ability to recover when something goes wrong.

So I would frame the question a little differently now: where does explicit structure help, and where should we let the system learn? I still think abstraction and planning are useful. But the abstractions have to be grounded in what the robot can reliably do, and the plan has to change based on what actually happens.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention the RT series or say the direction remains far from realization.

r002.rationale: The response presents grounding abstractions in what the robot can do as important, rather than judging deliberate language-to-action grounding to be unpromising.
